title: Module Preamble: Problem and the Key ZMod Identity
content: The module docstring precisely states the biconditional to be proved and the key insight that drives it: in ZMod d, the ring identity 9·R(k)+1=10^k holds exactly, transforming divisibility into a power-equality question. The repunit is defined privately by recursion: R(0)=0 and R(n+1)=R(n)·10+1, so R(k)=1+10+...+10^(k-1). The Lean imports bring in ZMod.Basic (for ZMod and natCast_eq_zero_iff), GroupTheory.OrderOfElement (for orderOf and orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one), and Mathlib.Tactic.
mathContext: $R(k) = \underbrace{11\ldots1}_{k} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} 10^i = \frac{10^k - 1}{9}$. In $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$: $9 \cdot R(k) + 1 = 10^k$. This identity avoids natural number subtraction and holds in any commutative ring where $10$ and $9$ are well-defined.

title: ZMod Ring Identity: 9·R(k)+1=10^k by Induction with linear_combination
content: The auxiliary theorem repunit_ZMod_aux proves 9·R(k)+1=10^k in any ZMod d by structural induction on k. The base case (k=0) uses simp to reduce R(0)=0 and 10^0=1, giving 9·0+1=1. The inductive step uses simp [repunit] to unfold R(n+1)=R(n)·10+1, then linear_combination 10*ih to close the goal algebraically. The key: `linear_combination` finds the right linear combination of the hypothesis (ih : 9·R(n)+1=10^n) to close 9·(R(n)·10+1)+1=10^(n+1).
mathContext: Inductive step: $9 \cdot R(n+1) + 1 = 9(R(n) \cdot 10 + 1) + 1 = 9R(n)\cdot 10 + 10 = (9R(n)+1)\cdot 10 = 10^n \cdot 10 = 10^{n+1}$. The `linear_combination 10 * ih` tactic proves $9 \cdot R(n+1) + 1 - 10^{n+1} = 10 \cdot (9 \cdot R(n) + 1 - 10^n) = 0$.

title: Main Theorem: Forward Direction (d ∣ R(k) → 10^k ≡ 1)
content: The main theorem repunit_dvd_iff_orderOf proves the biconditional by first rewriting both sides via Mathlib lemmas: ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff converts d∣R(k) to (R(k):ZMod d)=0, and orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one converts ord_d(10)∣k to (10:ZMod d)^k=1. The forward direction is then clean: if R(k)≡0, then 9·R(k)=0, so from the ring identity 9·R(k)+1=10^k we get 10^k=1.
mathContext: Forward direction: $(R(k): \mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}) = 0 \Rightarrow 9 \cdot R(k) = 0 \Rightarrow 10^k = 9 \cdot R(k) + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1$. The Lean proof uses `rw [hR, mul_zero, zero_add] at h10; exact h10.symm` where `h10 : 9·R(k)+1=10^k` is the ring identity instantiated at `d,k`.

title: Main Theorem: Backward Direction and Coprimality Role
content: The backward direction (10^k≡1 → d∣R(k)) requires the coprimality hypothesis gcd(d,9)=1. From 10^k=1 and the ring identity, we get 9·R(k)=0 in ZMod d, meaning d∣9·R(k) in ℕ. Since gcd(d,9)=1, Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left gives d∣R(k). This is why the theorem needs gcd(d,9)=1 rather than gcd(d,10)=1: d=3 satisfies gcd(3,10)=1 but ord_3(10)=1 and 3∤R(1)=1, so the backward direction would fail.
mathContext: Backward direction: $10^k \equiv 1 \pmod{d} \Rightarrow 9R(k) + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod{d} \Rightarrow 9R(k) \equiv 0 \pmod{d} \Rightarrow d \mid 9R(k)$. Then $\gcd(d,9)=1$ and `Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left` give $d \mid R(k)$. Counterexample: $d=3$, $k=1$: $10^1 = 10 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ so $\text{ord}_3(10)=1 \mid 1$, but $3 \nmid R(1)=1$. This fails because $\gcd(3,9)=3 \neq 1$.

title: Concrete Verifications via native_decide
content: Six examples verify the theorem for d=7, d=11, and d=37. The examples check both the positive cases (d∣R(k) for the correct k) and negative cases (d∤R(k) for k-1). The native_decide tactic delegates the computation to compiled Lean code, making it feasible for k up to ~6. These verify: ord_7(10)=6 (7∤R(1),R(2),R(3),R(4),R(5) but 7∣R(6)), ord_11(10)=2 (11∣R(2) but not R(1)), ord_37(10)=3 (37∣R(3) but not R(2)).
mathContext: $R(6) = 111111 = 7 \times 15873 \times 1$; $R(2) = 11 = 11 \times 1$; $R(3) = 111 = 3 \times 37$. The multiplicative orders $\text{ord}_7(10) = 6$, $\text{ord}_{11}(10) = 2$, $\text{ord}_{37}(10) = 3$ follow from: $10^6 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$ (since $10 \equiv 3$ and $3^6 = 729 \equiv 1$), $10^2 = 100 \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$, $10^3 = 1000 = 27 \times 37 + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod{37}$.
